segment_1.topic_phrase: what riding between lanes actually does to a rider's claim
segment_1.setup: I'm **{{INTERVIEWER}}**, and today we're talking about something a lot of Florida riders never get told straight. What riding between lanes actually does to your claim, and what to do if you get hit doing it.
segment_1.credential: **{{ATTORNEY}}**, after **{{YEARS_PRACTICING}}** years you know these judges, and you know exactly how the other side plays a case with a motorcycle in it.
segment_1.prompt: There's one thing about this that almost nobody gets told straight. Set us straight on it. And if getting it wrong has cost somebody real money, tell us about that one.

attributes.name: Tried in front of a jury
attributes.detail: Cases you took to a jury, and what changed once the jury had actually met your client.

attributes.name: Riders hit by cars
attributes.detail: Not injury cases generally. Motorcycle riders struck by drivers, how many, and how recently.

attributes.name: Record you can check
attributes.detail: Your license and your clean record with the Bar. That's checkable, and it's worth more than any badge on a website.

attributes.name: What a jury assumes here
attributes.detail: The county court, the judges, and the view a local jury tends to walk in with about motorcycles.

attributes.name: Countering rider bias
attributes.detail: How you take apart the assumption that the rider must have been doing something reckless.

attributes.name: Reading the damage
attributes.detail: Reconstructionists and treating physicians, and what the damage on both vehicles says about who did what.

attributes.name: Before the bike is scrapped
attributes.detail: What you go get in the first few days, because the bike gets scrapped and the security footage gets recorded over fast.

attributes.name: Every policy that could pay
attributes.detail: How you find coverage that matters more to a rider than to anyone else on the road.

attributes.name: The helmet argument
attributes.detail: How you handle it when there was no helmet, because the other side will lead with that.

attributes.name: The filing deadline
attributes.detail: Say the actual number of years out loud, and say what happens the day after it runs out.

attributes.name: Fees and the examination
attributes.detail: The percentage, whether it rises if you file suit, who pays to have the bike and the damage examined, and what happens if you lose.

attributes.name: When the rider's choice hurts
attributes.detail: When something the rider did genuinely damages the case, give them the number rather than a promise.

questions.q: What's lane-splitting, and how is it different from filtering, on US 1 and Kanner Highway?

bullets.label: Splitting is through moving traffic
bullets.detail: riding the line between two lanes of cars that are still going.

bullets.label: Filtering is at a standstill
bullets.detail: moving up between stopped cars at a light, at walking pace.

bullets.label: Neither one is legal here
bullets.detail: Florida bans both, and we get a lot of drivers and riders from out of state, so plenty of people are going off the rules from somewhere it's legal.

questions.q: If you were splitting lanes when you were hit in Stuart, is your case over?

bullets.label: No, and that's the important part
bullets.detail: breaking a traffic rule puts a share of the blame on you. It doesn't end your claim.

bullets.label: There's a cutoff
bullets.detail: past a certain share of the blame in Florida you recover nothing, so the size of that share is everything.

bullets.label: What it looks like locally
bullets.detail: on I-95 and the Turnpike, where traffic backs up and the temptation to move between lanes is real, and where the speeds make the outcome severe.

questions.q: How do insurance companies use lane-splitting to blame the rider?

bullets.label: They lead with it
bullets.detail: it's the first thing raised, often before anyone has established the rider was even doing it.

bullets.label: Assumption isn't evidence
bullets.detail: an adjuster will assume a rider on US 1 was moving between lanes because it's a convenient story, not because anyone saw it.

bullets.label: Make them prove it
bullets.detail: the position of the bike and the damage on both vehicles either support that story or they don't.

questions.q: What's rider bias, and how much does it actually cost people?

bullets.label: They decide before they read anything
bullets.detail: the adjuster has already made up their mind about what kind of person rides a motorcycle before they open the file.

bullets.label: It shows up as a fault percentage
bullets.detail: they assume the rider was speeding, they turn that assumption into a percentage, and they take it straight off what they pay.

bullets.label: You beat it with evidence, not argument
bullets.detail: reconstruction, the road itself, and the driver's own record are what actually change their mind.

questions.q: How much does being seen matter to fault in Stuart and across the Treasure Coast?

bullets.label: It's the standard defense
bullets.detail: the driver says they never saw the bike, like that settles it.

bullets.label: Not seeing isn't an excuse
bullets.detail: you've a duty to look, so a driver who says they never saw the bike has just admitted they weren't looking.

bullets.label: Where it really is hard to see a bike
bullets.detail: US 1 and Kanner Highway, where a rider sits low among larger vehicles and drivers are watching for gaps in traffic rather than for a bike.

questions.q: How does the left-turn crash happen to riders in Stuart?

bullets.label: It's the most common one
bullets.detail: a car turns across the rider's path because the driver misjudged the speed or never registered the bike.

bullets.label: The rider has nowhere to go
bullets.detail: there's no time to brake and no room to swerve once the car has committed.

bullets.label: Where it happens here
bullets.detail: the left turns off US 1 into the businesses along it, where a driver is eyeballing a gap and just doesn't see the bike at all.

questions.q: How is fault decided when a car rear-ends a motorcycle?

bullets.label: The driver in back starts on defense
bullets.detail: you're supposed to leave enough room to stop, so if you hit what's in front of you, you've some explaining to do.

bullets.label: They will still try
bullets.detail: the usual line is that the rider stopped suddenly or was hard to see.

bullets.label: The damage tells the story
bullets.detail: where the bike got hit and how far it went tell you most of what happened.

questions.q: What happens when a rider gets hit by an opening car door?

bullets.label: There's no avoiding it
bullets.detail: a door opens into the lane and the rider is on it before anything can be done.

bullets.label: Whoever opens the door owns it
bullets.detail: you look before you swing a door into traffic, and that goes for passengers too.

bullets.label: Where riders meet parked cars
bullets.detail: the parking along the downtown streets off US 1, where riders pass parked cars closely by necessity.

questions.q: How does a distracted driver end up hitting a rider?

bullets.label: A bike is easy to miss
bullets.detail: at a glance a motorcycle looks like a gap in traffic, especially to somebody looking at a phone.

bullets.label: It removes their defense
bullets.detail: a driver who never looked can't claim the rider came out of nowhere.

bullets.label: And we can check
bullets.detail: the phone records show exactly what that driver was doing in the seconds before the crash, and we can go get them.

questions.q: How does wearing a helmet, or not, affect a claim in Florida?

bullets.label: Adults have a choice here
bullets.detail: Florida doesn't require a helmet if you're over twenty-one and you carry the medical coverage the law requires.

bullets.label: They will still raise it
bullets.detail: on any head injury the other side will argue a helmet would have changed the outcome.

bullets.label: It can shrink the claim, not kill it
bullets.detail: the argument goes to the size of the head injury claim, and here a serious one means a transfer out of the county and a longer record to build.
